content: 1. The detection of anti-M. leprae PGL-I IgM antibodies in children is being considered as a potential diagnostic tool to evaluate the transmission of leprosy within a community. The optimal age group for testing remains to be determined. 2. The number of children in a given sample who test positive for anti-M. leprae PGL-I IgM antibodies, as well as the prevalence (percentage) of positive cases among the total number of children tested, can be used to monitor transmission trends over time. 3. Further research is recommended to explore the use of the PGL-I test as a diagnostic tool for assessing the interruption of leprosy transmission under programmatic conditions. 4. Surveillance and data management systems must be established to support disease control programs. These systems should include mechanisms for case notification, web-based reporting platforms, and mandatory reporting of sporadic cases. 5. Surveillance of diseases like poliomyelitis relies on tracking the number of cases presenting with acute flaccid paralysis as recorded in health services. 6. The application of data sets from four countries has largely validated the assumptions used to define cut-off points for leprosy elimination. Data from the Maldives and Morocco were reviewed, highlighting the potential for a return to pre-elimination status if clusters of cases occur. A cluster is defined as two cases in one year or cases in two consecutive years within a single second-level subnational jurisdiction. However, if these cases are determined to be unrelated, they can be classified as sporadic without reversing elimination status. 7. Sporadic cases, including those in children, may occur even after leprosy elimination has been declared. These cases do not appear to lead to a resurgence of the disease. Each sporadic case should undergo a critical incident investigation to determine its origin and implications. 8. Countries are expected to conduct subnational-level assessments to evaluate the interruption of transmission and elimination of leprosy. Reports from these assessments should be included in the national dossier. 9. Long-term assessment surveys (LTAS) are recommended for countries to: Evaluate the interruption of transmission at all second-tier subnational units using internal teams. Assess the elimination of leprosy at all second-tier subnational units using internal teams. Verify the elimination of leprosy at the national level with external teams, such as those from the World Health Organization (WHO). 10. Detailed technical guidance will be provided to countries on topics such as LTAS protocols, reporting, the development of a country dossier to claim disease elimination, and critical incident investigations for sporadic cases. 11. Zoonotic transmission of leprosy should be investigated, particularly the potential role of nine-banded armadillos in the Americas. Additionally, leprosy caused by Mycobacterium lepromatosis, a pathogen similar to M. leprae, should also be considered. 12. A series of meetings and consultations were held to define criteria, concepts, and indicators for the interruption of transmission and elimination of leprosy. These included discussions on epidemiological indicators, programmatic criteria, and the feasibility of leprosy elimination assessment surveys (LEAS). 13. Surveillance and response systems are critical for achieving the interruption of transmission, elimination of leprosy, and post-elimination monitoring. Templates and content for national dossiers were discussed to ensure comprehensive documentation. 14. The meetings concluded with the development of guidance for national programs on verifying disease elimination, creating dossiers, and managing data at subnational levels. Recommendations for next steps were provided to ensure progress toward leprosy elimination goals.
